title: Constitutional Provisions Embodying the Rule of Law

content.overview: The Indian Constitution embodies the rule of law through supremacy of the Constitution, equality before law, separation of powers, fundamental rights and judicial review. Leading decisions have treated the rule of law as part of the basic structure.
content.glance: Identify the constitutional provision or principle engaged (equality, judicial review, supremacy of the Constitution) and explain how it operationalises the rule of law on the facts.
content.study: Rule of law in the constitutional sense means that all power is exercised under and according to the Constitution and law. Articles 14, 21, 32 and 226, the independence of the judiciary and the basic-structure doctrine give institutional shape to this idea. Arbitrary power is antithetical to the constitutional order. Landmark decisions have affirmed that the rule of law is a basic feature that cannot be abrogated by amendment. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Constitutional Supremacy
sections.body: All organs of the State derive power from and are limited by the Constitution.

sections.heading: Equality and Non-Arbitrariness
sections.body: Article 14 condemns arbitrary state action and requires reasoned, non-discriminatory exercise of power.

sections.heading: Judicial Review
sections.body: Courts enforce constitutional limits through Articles 32 and 226.

sections.heading: Basic Structure
sections.body: The rule of law has been recognised as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Application
sections.body: Every exercise of public power must be traceable to law and consistent with constitutional guarantees.

examples.title: Arbitrary executive order
examples.body: An executive order imposes a burden without legal authorisation or relevant criteria. Article 14 and constitutional supremacy are engaged.

examples.title: Attempt to oust judicial review
examples.body: A measure seeks to immunise state action from all judicial scrutiny. Basic-structure limits on destroying judicial review are engaged.

hypotheticals.question: Does rule of law only mean that laws are published?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. It also requires non-arbitrariness, equality and effective review.

hypotheticals.question: Can Parliament abolish judicial review by ordinary law?
hypotheticals.analysis: Judicial review of constitutional limits is a basic feature and cannot be abrogated.

distinctions.title: Constitutional rule of law vs Diceyan formulation
distinctions.left: Grounded in the written Constitution and basic structure
distinctions.right: Classical English emphasis on ordinary law and absence of wide discretionary power

misconceptions.trap: Rule of law means only that laws are published.
misconceptions.correction: It also requires non-arbitrariness, equality and effective review.

misconceptions.trap: Parliament can abolish judicial review by ordinary law.
misconceptions.correction: Judicial review of constitutional limits is a basic feature.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.facts: Constitutional amendments and the extent of Parliament's amending power.
cases.issue: What constitutional limitations govern amendment power?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution has a basic structure that cannot be destroyed by amendment.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on constitutional supremacy and rule of law as basic structure.

cases.name: Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi v Shri Raj Narain
cases.issue: Whether essential constitutional principles may be displaced by amendment.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Rule of law, democracy and judicial review are integral to the constitutional structure.
cases.holding: Impugned provisions invalid to the extent they damaged basic constitutional principles.
cases.relevance: Authority already in the file on rule of law and constitutional limitations.

cases.name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) by LRs. v State of Tamil Nadu
cases.facts: Ninth Schedule immunity against judicial review.
cases.issue: Whether constitutional insulation from review is unlimited.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Post-Kesavananda Ninth Schedule laws remain reviewable on basic-structure grounds.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a constitutional rule-of-law problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify constitutional provision engaged. II. Apply equality/non-arbitrariness. III. Note judicial review. IV. Address basic-structure limits if amendment is in issue.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Constitutional source; non-arbitrariness analysis; judicial-review pathway; basic-structure argument if relevant.
